Suitability of Technical Analysis Highly suitable due to stable short-term fundamentals. Less likely to be suitable, as past trends in share prices become unreliable for understanding subsequent movements.

docs.title: 4.4.1 Core Premise and Philosophy
docs.text:
Long-Term Focus: Unlike technical analysis, fundamental analysis is focused exclusively on long-term investing.

Value Drivers: Operates on the premise that since equity shares reflect part ownership of a company, its long-term value must be driven by the profits and cash flows generated by the company on its investments.

Market Mispricing: If short-term price movements cause the market price to significantly diverge from its fair value, it creates a profit-making opportunity.

Contradiction to EMH: This philosophy directly contradicts the Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH), which propagates that share prices continuously incorporate and reflect all relevant information.

docs.title: 4.4.2 Investment Decision Matrix
docs.text:
Profits in investments depend not only on identifying a good investment option but also on making the investment at the right price. Analysts determine actions by comparing the market price to the estimated fair value (intrinsic value):

Market Condition Valuation Assessment Recommended Action Market Price < Intrinsic Value The stock is undervalued; represents an attractive investment opportunity. Buy / Hold Market Price > Intrinsic Value The stock is overvalued; market price is above the fair price of the business. Sell / Avoid

docs.title: 4.4.3 The Three Framework Baskets (E-I-C Analysis)
docs.text: Fundamental analysis involves a comprehensive study of a company’s business operations and governance style. All key analytical questions are grouped into three structured baskets:

docs.title: Economic Analysis
docs.text:
• Gauges the overall cyclical and secular macroeconomic trends.
  • Evaluates whether the broader economic environment is likely to help the industry grow or cause it to decline.

docs.title: Industry Analysis
docs.text:
• Examines the competitive intensity within the specific industry.
  • Evaluates whether the prevailing industry dynamics are conducive for existing players to thrive.

docs.title: Company Analysis
docs.text:
Competitive Positioning: Analyzes how the company is positioned vis-à-vis its direct competitors and whether it will perform better or worse than them.

Cost Structure: Evaluates the company's cost structure and how it is likely to impact profitability under different business environments.

Financial Health: Reviews the strength of the company’s financial position to see if it can fund future growth or withstand an operational crisis.

Management Capabilities: Assesses whether the management can identify and execute the right strategies to exploit growth opportunities while defending the business from adversities.

Corporate Governance: Verifies if the right governance structure is present to ensure that the board of directors and management act in the best interest of shareholders.

docs.title: Core Philosophy and Definition
docs.text:
Data-Driven Approach: Quantitative research applies strict mathematical frameworks, statistical tests, and rule-based data screens to historical records. This method eliminates human emotion, subjectivity, and cognitive variance from the selection cycle.

Cross-Disciplinary Application: This approach can be integrated into both major research methods:

  1. In Technical Analysis: Analysts bypass reading visual charts entirely and focus purely on the underlying data. They study statistical relationships between price up-moves, down-moves, trading volume, and other parameters to gauge the direction of stock prices.

  2. In Fundamental Analysis: While traditional fundamental research involves a blend of both quantitative and qualitative studies, some analysts approach equity analysis from a purely quantitative perspective.

docs.title: Methodological Tools and Projections
docs.text:
To project future earnings, valuations, and financial performance, quantitative analysts utilize a progressive suite of tools:

  • Time Series Analysis & Regression: Used at the simplest level to analyze historical finance and operational metrics to extrapolate future earnings.
  • Econometric Approaches: Sophisticated econometric and statistical methodologies are utilized to refine output data.
  • Financial Statement Analysis Tools: Applied to project future financials and calculate corporate growth rates.
  • Sensitivity Analysis & Simulations: Programmatic tests executed to isolate and understand the impact of modifying key baseline assumptions on asset valuations.

docs.title: Essential Quantitative Metrics, Equations, and Screens
docs.text:
Quantitative analysis relies heavily on specific statistical formulas and automated screens to isolate financial indicators:

  • Asset Price Volatility (\(\sigma\)): The statistical standard deviation of a security's historical returns, serving as the benchmark measurement for total investment risk exposure.
  • Systematic Risk Coefficient (\(\beta\)): Measures the volatility of a security (\(R_i\)) relative to the broader market index portfolio (\(R_m\)):
\[\beta = \frac{\text{Covariance}(R_i, R_m)}{\text{Variance}(R_m)}\]
  • The Sharpe Ratio (Risk-Adjusted Outperformance Evaluation): Measures the structural excess return generated by an investment portfolio (\(R_p\)) per unit of its total standard deviation risk exposure (\(\sigma_p\)), where \(R_f\) is the risk-free benchmark rate:
\[\text{Sharpe Ratio} = \frac{R_p - R_f}{\sigma_p}\]
  • Systematic Factor Screeners: Programmatic filters applied to clean institutional databases to automatically extract target securities based on fixed parameters.
Sample Screener Parameter Target Criteria Operational Rationale Cash Conversion Screen \(\text{Operating Cash Flow / Net Profit Ratio} \ge 1.0\) Identifies strong earnings quality and high cash generation. Profitability Screen \(\text{Return on Equity (ROE)} > 20\%\) Filters for highly efficient equity capital deployment. Leverage Screen \(\text{Debt-to-Equity Ratio} < 0.5\) Isolates companies with low financial risk exposure.

docs.title: Core Strategic Limitations
docs.text:
Despite its mathematical precision, applying a pure quantitative or econometric approach to fundamental analysis suffers from major structural limitations:

  • Availability of Comparable Data: Frequent changes in accounting standards and shifting corporate business models make historical past data less useful when compared with present market conditions.
  • Conclusion: Due to these historical data discrepancies, a pure quantitative research approach is not often employed in isolation for comprehensive fundamental analysis.

docs.title: Core Premise and Philosophy
docs.text:
• Psychological Influence: Investment decisions are ideally based on the analysis of available information to reflect expected performance and risks. However, very often decisions are heavily influenced by the behavioral biases of the decision maker, leading to less than optimal choices being made.
  • Fear and Greed Driving Prices: Proponents of behavioral finance integrate psychological insight with financial economics. They assume that securities' prices drift away from their fair fundamental values (either to the upside or downside) due to the systemic fear and greed of market participants.

docs.title: High-Level Behavioral Anomalies
docs.text:
The specific psychological flaws and emotional biases that alter rational investment cycles include:

  • Herd Mentality: Driven by the psychological pressure to copy the collective behavior of the crowd. This fuels structural asset bubbles during market upswings out of the fear of missing out and accelerates severe market crashes through collective panic-selling.
  • Anchoring Bias: A cognitive flaw where an investor or analyst weights their valuation expectations too heavily toward an arbitrary historical benchmark—such as a stock's past all-time high or its initial purchase price—failing to update their outlook even as current business fundamentals decay.
  • Loss Aversion: Rooted in the reality that the psychological pain of booking a financial loss is roughly twice as intense as the utility derived from making an equivalent profit gain. This emotional imbalance causes investors to hold onto declining, value-destructive positions in the hope of breaking even, while selling winning positions prematurely.
  • Overconfidence Bias: Involves underestimating downside probability distributions while overestimating forecasting precision. This bias frequently leads to over-trading, excessive leverage, and a relaxed attitude toward essential risk metrics.

Cross-Reference Note: While this section serves as an essential framework overview within the fundamentals of research, a more comprehensive analysis of these well-documented behavioral biases and their direct influence on market decision-making is covered in detail in Chapter 11.

docs.title: Core Philosophy and Definition
docs.text:
• Market Mechanics: Fundamental analysis in commodities is the study of economic, political, and natural factors that influence the supply and demand of commodities, thereby determining their price movements.
  • Analytical Scope: Rather than focusing on corporate earnings or financial metrics, commodity fundamental analysis largely focuses on the structural dynamics of physical goods. This includes the study of supply and demand factors, seasonality, macroeconomic conditions, news, currency movements, interest rates, weather, inventory levels, and government intervention.

docs.title: Supply-Side Dynamics
docs.text:
The key supply-side factors that restrict or expand the physical availability of a commodity, influencing market fluctuations, include:

  1. Production: Direct output volumes originating from farms (agricultural products), oil wells (energy), and mines (metals).
  2. Weather Conditions: Sudden natural events such as floods, droughts, and cyclonic effects that physically disrupt crop yields or extraction operations.
  3. Government Policies: Regulatory actions including tariffs, levies, subsidies, and strict trade restrictions or promotions.
  4. Geopolitical Events: Structural disruptions caused by sanctions, wars, and international trade disputes.
  5. Input Costs: Changes in operating overheads, including energy costs, raw input costs, labor wages, and technological adaptations.

docs.title: Demand-Side Dynamics
docs.text:
The key consumption drivers that influence global demand and cause commodity market fluctuations include:

  1. Global Economic Growth: Improvements in global GDP accelerate industrial activity, creating additional demand for base metals, energy resources, and agricultural products.
  2. Population Growth & Urbanization: Structural expansions in population sizes and city developments that permanently increase global food and energy consumption scales.
  3. Substitution Effect: The economic choice of switching between alternative commodities when relative prices fluctuate.
  4. Seasonal Demand: Predictable consumption spikes, such as higher heating fuel demand in winter, cooling fuel demand in summer, or specific festive food demand.
  5. Consumer Preferences: Long-term secular shifts in purchasing habits, such as transitions to organic foods, renewable energy systems, and electric vehicles.

docs.title: Macroeconomic Indicators
docs.text:
Broader macroeconomic signals establish price trends across financialized commodity markets:

Macroeconomic Indicator Market Mechanism Financial Effect on Commodities Inflation Commodities possess intrinsic physical value. Precious metals (especially Gold and Silver) are heavily utilized as an inflation hedge to protect purchasing power. Positively Correlated (Prices tend to rise with high inflation) Interest Rates Higher global interest rates alter capital flows and typically strengthen the United States Dollar (USD). Since global commodities are priced in USD, a stronger dollar increases buying costs abroad. Negatively Correlated (Higher rates typically lower commodity prices) Trade Balance & Industrial Data Economic metrics such as the Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) and Industrial Production data indicate industrial manufacturing health, directly altering the consumption velocity of base metals and energy. Direct Indicator (Strong industrial data boosts industrial commodity demand)

docs.title: 1. Macroeconomic Role and Core Characteristics
docs.text:
Gold operates under unique economic principles compared to traditional corporate securities. Research findings demonstrate that it carries a structural inverse relationship with equities, bonds, and fiat currencies.

  • The Safe-Haven Phenomenon: During macro-systemic downturns or environments of severe economic turbulence when traditional capital markets underperform, investors systematically migrate capital into gold to preserve value.
  • Inflation Hedging: Because it functions as a tangible store of value, gold serves as a physical buffer against currency degradation and inflationary pressures.

docs.title: 2. Sectoral Demand Breakdown
docs.text:
An analysis of the global structural demand allocation indicates that consumption is heavily driven by retail storage and monetary institutional support rather than industrial application:

Sector Allocation (%) Structural Characterization Jewellery 47% The primary demand anchor, heavily influenced by retail consumer behavior and seasonal/cultural patterns. Investment 24% Financialized demand (e.g., bar/coin hoarding or ETF buying) driven by wealth preservation motives. Central Bank 23% Institutional reserves accumulation used to diversify national holdings away from fiat credit risk. Technology 6% Minor industrial component representing physical usage in electronics or specialized applications.

docs.title: 3. Geographic Concentration of Supply and Demand
docs.text:
The structural balance of global gold markets is concentrated within a few major nations. A core finding is that China holds a dual position as the world's leading physical extraction source and its largest final consumer market.

Market Position Dominant Geographies (Ranked 1 to 5) Major Producers China, Australia, Russia, USA, Canada Major Consumers China, India, USA, Germany, Saudi Arabia

docs.title: 4. Price Driving Factors and Market Mechanisms
docs.text:
Gold price discovery relies on identifying changes across interest rates, macroeconomic metrics, currency valuations, and capital market performance:

  • Monetary Policy & Yield Environments: Lower bond yields or an expansionary monetary policy (lowering interest rates) act as positive price triggers (+). Conversely, contracting monetary policies (interest rate hikes) or higher bond yields act as negative price triggers (-) by raising the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset.
  • The Dollar Correlation: Gold maintains a strict negative correlation with the global reserve currency. A weaker U.S. Dollar decreases purchasing barriers globally, serving as a positive trigger (+), whereas a stronger U.S. Dollar serves as a negative trigger (-).
  • Economic Data & Risk Sentiment: Weaker macroeconomic metrics (declining GDP, slowing manufacturing, or weakening labor reports) and bearish equity trends signal systemic stress, functioning as positive triggers (+) for gold due to safe-haven inflows. Stronger economic growth and a bullish stock market cause capital to exit gold for higher-risk assets, working as negative triggers (-).
  • Institutional Flow Tracking: Programmatic institutional accumulation through Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) or direct Central Bank buying systematically builds a structural demand floor, providing positive price triggers (+), while net liquidations or selling activity create negative pressures (-).

docs.title: 1. Macroeconomic Role and Core Characteristics
docs.text:
Crude Oil is traditionally termed the "mother of the global financial market" or "black gold" due to its pervasive role in underwriting global industrial activity and economic expansion.

  • Economic Lifeline: Naturally occurring as a highly flammable liquid within subsurface rock formations, its primary value is unlocked via fractional distillation at varying temperatures. This process yields critical downstream industrial components: bitumen (road asphalt), lubricants, fuel oil, diesel, paraffin, naphtha, and gasoline.
  • The Inflation Transmission Vector: Because transport fuels and polymers (plastics for consumer goods, bottles, and packaging) act as raw inputs across nearly all global economic supply chains, any supply-demand imbalance in the crude oil market instantly translates into cross-border inflationary concerns.

docs.title: 2. Structural Quality and Quality Benchmarks
docs.text:
Crude oil price discovery is highly dependent on physical grading specifications, which are benchmarked against two primary variables: Density and Sulphur Content:

  • West Texas Intermediate (WTI): A light, low-sulphur ("sweet") crude oil benchmark predominantly explored and physically settled within the United States. It possesses an API gravity of \(39^\circ\) and a minimal Sulphur content of \(0.24\%\). It is financialized and traded primarily on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX).
  • Brent Oil: The premier international pricing benchmark used to value crude supplies moving out of Europe, Africa, and the Middle East, originating from the United Kingdom's North Sea fields. It has an API gravity of \(38^\circ\) and a Sulphur content of \(0.4\%\). It is financialized and traded primarily on the Intercontinental Exchange (ICE).

docs.title: 3. Geopolitical Supply Control and Market Concentration
docs.text:
Global energy distribution is heavily impacted by strict cartelized production and geographical infrastructure limitations:

  • The OPEC+ Dominance: Global crude supply lines are tightly managed by a duopoly consisting of the United States and the OPEC+ coalition (comprising 13 formal OPEC member nations plus aligned external producers, led by Russia).
  • Reserve Concentration: The Middle East holds a commanding structural bottleneck, accounting for 48% of all proven global oil reserves. Within this footprint, OPEC alone controls roughly 40% of ongoing global production, acts as the custodian for 75% of total proven world reserves, and commands 55% of the international oil export market.

docs.title: 4. Geographic Concentration of Production and Consumption
docs.text:
The physical flow of energy highlights the massive industrial reliance of expanding Asian economies (specifically China and India) on foreign energy inputs, contrasted with the United States' unique position as both the top global producer and consumer:

Market Position Dominant Geographies (Ranked 1 to 5) Major Producers USA, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Canada, China Major Consumers USA, China, India, Germany, Japan

docs.title: 5. Price Driving Factors and Market Mechanisms
docs.text:
Crude oil behaves as an industrial asset, meaning its price discovery runs inversely to safe-haven assets like gold:

  • Supply Manipulation and Infrastructure Tracking: Tightening production quotas by the OPEC+ group, drops in domestic U.S. output, falling active U.S. oil rig counts, or shrinking U.S. commercial inventory levels all shrink total available supply, functioning as positive price triggers (+). Increases in production quotas, rising rig counts, or expanding commercial inventories act as negative price triggers (-).
  • Macroeconomic Health & Capital Benchmarks: Unlike gold, expanding macroeconomic metrics (booming GDP growth, rising industrial output indices, and bullish equity markets) signify a direct acceleration in industrial energy consumption, acting as positive price triggers (+). Economic contractions or bearish stock trends compress demand, serving as negative price triggers (-).
  • Exogenous Disruptions (Weather and Geopolitics): Unstable political environments within the Middle East or severe weather patterns in production hubs (such as the hurricane season across the Gulf of Mexico) threaten infrastructure continuity and trigger risk premiums, acting as positive price triggers (+). A return to political stability or calm weather patterns functions as a negative price trigger (-).
  • The Dollar Denomination Effect: Because global crude oil is invoiced and settled internationally in U.S. Dollars (USD), currency movements shift physical buying power. A weaker USD acts as a positive price trigger (+) by making oil cheaper for foreign purchasers, whereas a strengthening USD functions as a negative price trigger (-).

docs.title: Case Analysis: The Negative Oil Pricing Anomaly (April 20, 2020)
Operational Facts & Market Dynamics
docs.text:
• The Event: On April 20, 2020, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude oil prices collapsed below zero, entering negative territory for the first time in history.
  • Exogenous Catalyst: Roughly 90% of the global economy was placed under strict pandemic-induced lockdown restrictions to curb the spread of coronavirus, completely destroying immediate physical fuel demand.
  • Contractual Bottleneck: The WTI futures contract for May delivery was scheduled to expire on the subsequent day (April 21, 2020). WTI is a physically deliverable contract legally tied to the infrastructure hub at Cushing, Oklahoma.
  • The Valuation Collapse: Due to lockdown-induced logistical restrictions on moving physical oil, combined with near-capacity local storage facilities, speculative buyers and financial participants holding the expiring contracts were completely unable or unwilling to take physical delivery.
  • The Pricing Rationale: To escape the legal and financial obligations of physical delivery, contract holders engaged in extreme panic selling. Buyers essentially paid counter-parties to take the oil contracts off their hands, overriding traditional cost-of-production pricing floors and forcing market clearing prices below zero.

docs.title: Historical Parallel: The 1973 Cartel Shock
docs.text:
The 2020 demand-collapse crisis stands in stark contrast to the structural supply shock of 1973. During this post-World War II crisis, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) wielded its market power to drastically alter the global energy landscape:

  • Pricing Action: OPEC unilaterally quadrupled oil prices, raising them to approximately $12 a barrel.
  • Embargo Execution: The cartel placed an outright prohibition on oil exports to the United States, Japan, and Western Europe—nations that collectively consumed over half of the global oil supply at the time. This action solidified crude oil's status as a critical geopolitical transmission mechanism.

docs.title: 4.10 Impact of Commodity Market on Equity Market
The Input Cost Transmission Mechanism
docs.text:
Commodity and equity markets maintain a close relationship because listed corporations rely heavily on raw commodities as industrial inputs. Changes in upstream commodity pricing flow directly into corporate income statements:

  • Rising Commodity Prices: Function as an input cost shock. This compresses corporate gross and net profit margins, causing downward adjustments in corporate earnings expectations and stock valuations.
  • Falling Commodity Prices: Act as an operating cost relief. This expands profit margins, improves corporate profitability, and drives upward stock valuation adjustments.

docs.title: Sectoral Divergence Matrix (Crude Oil Example)
docs.text:
A change in a core commodity does not impact the equity market uniformly; it creates distinct winners and losers depending on a sector's position relative to the raw input:

Sector Type Strategic Position Structural Mechanism Equity Market Impact Upstream Producers (e.g., Oil Exploration & Production) Input Seller Rising commodity prices increase revenues directly against a fixed operational cost base. Positive Impact (+) Profitability improves Downstream Consumers (e.g., Airlines & Logistics) Input Buyer Rising commodity prices escalate fuel, manufacturing, and transport overheads. Negative Impact (-) Profitability declines

docs.title: Commodities as Global Macroeconomic Signals
docs.text:
Because commodities are globally traded, physical price discovery serves as a leading indicator for systemic demand shifts. Equity markets are sensitive to economic growth prospects and react dynamically to these signals:

The Industrial Demand Signal:

  • Physical industrial metals reflect structural manufacturing momentum.

Case Study Example (Copper):

  • A significant fall in copper prices typically flags a broader contraction in global industrial and manufacturing demand.
  • Equity markets read this signal early, dragging down metal, mining, manufacturing, and core infrastructure stocks ahead of lagging official economic data.

docs.title: Key Takeaways:
docs.text:
Here is a brief summary of the key takeaways from Chapter 4 (Fundamentals of Research) - Major Sections:

Ethical Boundary & Research:

Analysts are strictly prohibited from utilizing material, non-public insider information (which immediately affects investment decisions). However, collecting individual pieces of public/non-public details and piecing them together to gain critical insights—known as Mosaic Analysis—is fully acceptable.

Technical Analysis Framework:

Focuses entirely on forecasting short-term price directions by reading historical Price and Volume patterns on charts. It operates on the core axiom that the market discounts everything (all fundamentals and sentiments are already reflected in the stock price).

Fundamental Analysis (Equity):

Focused on long-term investing under the premise that stock value is driven by corporate profits and cash flows. Investors capitalize on mispricing by buying when the market price falls below a business's intrinsic value and selling when it rises above it, utilizing E-I-C (Economic, Industry, Company) Analysis.

Quantitative Research:

Relies on strict mathematical frameworks, statistical equations (like Volatility \(\sigma\), Systematic Risk \(\beta\), and the Sharpe Ratio), and rule-based data screeners to remove human emotion. It is rarely used in isolation for fundamental analysis due to historical data discrepancies caused by changing accounting standards.

Behavioural Finance Approach:

Proves that market participants are not perfectly rational and are driven by psychological fear and greed. This creates systematic biases—such as Herd Mentality, Anchoring Bias, Loss Aversion, and Overconfidence—which temporarily push security prices away from their fair values.

Fundamental Analysis (Commodities):

Unlike equities, commodity research focuses on the physical supply-demand balance, weather events, geopolitical tensions, macro indicators (inflation and interest rates), and storage inventory rather than corporate financial health.

  • Asset-Specific Drivers (Gold vs. Crude Oil): * Gold acts as a safe haven and inflation hedge, moving inversely to traditional equities and bonds.

  • Crude Oil serves as the industrial lifeline of the global economy, directly affecting cross-border inflation and causing divergent sectoral equity movements (boosting upstream energy producers while hurting downstream consumers like airlines).

Historical Anomalies & Transmission:

Exogenous events can warp standard financial rules, as seen in the April 2020 negative WTI crude pricing caused by pandemic storage lockdowns and contract expiry rules. Ultimately, commodity price shifts serve as leading macro indicators that directly impact equity market valuations and profit margins.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Economic Analysis
docs.text: Economics is the study of how individuals and societies make choices under conditions of scarcity. It begins with the assumption that people are rational actors with well-defined goals who must face trade-offs because resources—both human and material—are limited. Economic analysis is typically divided into two branches: Microeconomics (focused on individual units) and Macroeconomics (focused on the aggregate economy).

docs.title: 5.1 Basic Principles of Microeconomics
docs.text:
Microeconomics studies the behavior of individuals and firms in making decisions regarding the allocation of scarce resources.

  • Consumer Demand: It posits that prices and production levels are driven by what individuals choose to buy and consume.

  • Theory of the Firm: It examines how individual businesses adopt strategies related to inputs, outputs, and production levels to maximize profits.

  • Price Determination: It explains how the interaction between producers and consumers determines the prices of specific goods and services.

docs.title: 5.2 Basic Principles of Macroeconomics
docs.text:
Macroeconomics focuses on "the big picture" by examining factors that influence the aggregate supply and demand of an entire nation.

  • Key Focus Areas: Analysts track aggregate variables such as the Gross Domestic Product (GDP), unemployment rates, national savings, and overall inflation levels.

  • Policy Influence: Macroeconomic performance is heavily influenced by Fiscal Policy (government spending and taxes) and Monetary Policy (central bank actions regarding money supply and interest rates).

docs.title: 5.3 Introduction to Various Macroeconomic Variables
docs.text: Policy makers strive for economic stability through low unemployment, price stability (low inflation), and steady growth.

docs.title: I. National Income (GDP and GNP)
docs.text:
National income is the primary measure of an economy's performance.

  • Gross Domestic Product (GDP): The market value of all final goods and services produced within a country’s borders, regardless of the nationality of the producer.

  • Gross National Product (GNP): The market value of goods and services produced by a country's residents, regardless of where they are located in the world.

  • Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA): The difference between GDP and GNP (\(GNP = GDP + NFIA\)).

Methods of Measuring GDP

Method Approach Calculation Basis Product Method Sector-wise Output Sum of the money value of all "final goods" produced in sectors like agriculture, industry, and services. Income Method Aggregate Income Sum of all wages/salaries (employees), professional fees, profits (entrepreneurs), and rent/interest (investors). Expenditure Method Consumption Sum of private consumption, government spending, gross capital formation, and net exports.

docs.title: II. Savings and Investments
docs.text:
Savings represent the portion of income not spent on current consumption.

  • Constituents: National saving is the sum of personal savings (individuals), corporate savings (undistributed profits), and public savings (government).

  • Conversion: Savings are channelled into Investments through financial instruments like equity and bonds to fund productive activities.

docs.title: III. Inflation and Interest Rates
docs.text:
Inflation is the general increase in price levels leading to the erosion of the purchasing power of money.

  • Demand-Pull Inflation: Caused by demand exceeding available supply.

  • Cost-Push Inflation: Caused by an increase in the cost of inputs (raw materials, labor).

  • Measurement: Tracked via the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) and the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

  • Relationship with Rates: Higher inflation often forces central banks to raise interest rates to encourage saving and cool down consumption.

docs.title: IV. Capital Flows: FDI and FPI
docs.text: Feature Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) Nature Active and stable; long-term commitment. Passive and volatile; "hot money". Control Investing entities participate in management decisions. Investment in markets (equity/bonds) without management involvement. Benefits Job creation, new technology, and managerial skills. Provides liquidity to the local capital markets.

docs.title: V. Fiscal Policy
docs.text:
Fiscal policy involves government decisions regarding revenue (taxation) and expenditure (infrastructure, welfare).

  • Fiscal Deficit: Occurs when the government's expenditure exceeds its recurring revenue; it is bridged through market borrowings.

  • Current Account Deficit (CAD): The difference between recurring revenue receipts from abroad and payments made to entities abroad. A high CAD can weaken a nation's currency.

Types of Fiscal Policy Stances

Policy Stance Condition Action Expansionary Recession / Slow growth Lower taxes and higher spending to put money in the hands of citizens. Contractionary High Inflation / Overheating Higher taxes and lower spending to cool the economy. Neutral Equilibrium Income and expenditure are balanced; no major changes needed.

docs.title: VI. Monetary Policy
docs.text:
Administered by the central bank (RBI in India), it manages money supply and interest rates.

Common Monetary Policy Tools

Tool Description Repo Rate The rate at which the RBI lends money to banks against securities. Reverse Repo The rate at which the RBI borrows money from banks against securities. Bank Rate The rate for long-term lending to banks without collateral. CRR & SLR Cash Reserve Ratio (cash held with RBI) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (liquid assets like gold/G-Secs held by banks).

docs.title: 5.4 Role of Economic Analysis in Fundamental Analysis
docs.text:
Economic analysis provides the context for evaluating a business's growth potential.

  • External Environment: GDP growth rates indicate the health of the broader market, while inflation and interest rates reveal the cost of capital and consumption strength.

  • Policy Room: High inflation or a large fiscal deficit can signal that the government or central bank has little room to stimulate the economy further.

docs.title: 5.5 Secular, Cyclical, and Seasonal Trends
docs.text:
Economic movements are categorized by their duration and predictability.

  • Secular Trends: Long-term shifts (7–10 years) often caused by technological disruptions, demographic changes, or cultural shifts (e.g., digitalization).

  • Seasonal Trends: Highly predictable annual patterns linked to weather or agriculture (e.g., higher GDP contribution from agriculture during harvest seasons).

  • Cyclical Trends: Medium-term fluctuations (2–6 years) that reverse over time.

The Four Phases of the Economic Cycle

  1. Expansion (Boom): Characterized by high consumer confidence, increased production, and rising inflation/interest rates.

  2. Slow Down: Higher prices and interest rates begin to discourage consumption; capacity utilization rates start to fall.

  3. Recession: Declining consumption leads to layoffs and falling interest rates/inflation; businesses halt expansion.

  4. Recovery: Low inflation allows for loose monetary policy; economic activity picks up as consumers begin buying again.

docs.title: Quick Facts for Revision
docs.text:
• Standard of Living: Per Capita Income (National Income / Total Population) is a better measure of standard of living than total GDP.

  • Service Sector: Constitutes approximately 60% of India's GDP at factor cost.

  • BOP Structure: The Balance of Payments now follows the IMF (BPM6) structure, dividing transactions into Current, Capital, and Financial accounts.

  • Globalization: The ability to produce and sell anything anywhere; it promotes resource efficiency but increases the risk of "contagion" from global crises.

  • Inventory Cycle: Short-term fluctuations within a commodity cycle caused by producers or customers adjusting their stock levels.

  • Key Information Sources: Major sources include government websites (RBI, SEBI, MOF), the Economic Survey, and published research reports.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Industry Analysis
docs.text: Industry analysis acts as the critical bridge between macro-economic analysis and individual company research. While economic analysis determines if the overall environment is growing, industry analysis identifies which specific sectors will thrive or struggle within that environment.

docs.title: 6.1 Role of Industry Analysis in Fundamental Research
docs.text:
Industry analysis evaluates the specific external factors that influence a group of similar businesses. Analysts must address several key questions:

  • Industry Definition: What exactly is the industry scope?

  • Cyclicality: How sensitive is the sector to economic booms and busts?

  • Market Sizing: What is the potential for growth versus current penetration?

  • Competitive Landscape: What is the level of rivalry and pricing power?

  • Value Migration: Are secular trends shifting profit from one sector to another?

docs.title: 6.2 Defining the Industry and Sectors
docs.text:
Defining an industry is challenging because standard classification systems like the National Industry Classification (NIC) or Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) may not capture the competitive substance of a business.

Term Scope Example Economic Sector Broad segments of the national income. Agriculture, Manufacturing, Services. Business Sector A broad category of related industries. Financial Services (includes Banking, Insurance, etc.). Industry Firms offering similar products to serve the same need. Auto Industry, Steel Industry.

The Definition Challenge:

Analysts must look beyond product types to customer needs. For example, PVR Limited can be defined narrowly as a "Cinema Exhibitor" or broadly as "Out of Home (OOH) Entertainment," which includes live theater and sporting leagues. Similarly, the camera industry was disrupted because it failed to recognize competition from mobile phones.

docs.title: 6.3 Understanding Industry Cyclicality
docs.text:
Industries are categorized by their "income elasticity," or how much demand changes when consumer income rises or falls.

  1. Defensive Industries: Products with low income elasticity. Demand remains stable regardless of the economy (e.g., Healthcare, Food, Agricultural inputs).

  2. Semi-Cyclical Industries: Experience growth during booms and decline during recessions but maintain a "base level" of demand (e.g., Consumer Durables).

  3. Deep Cyclical Industries: Highly sensitive to economic and commodity cycles. They suffer during recessions but see massive growth during recovery due to pent-up demand (e.g., Capital Goods, Steel).

docs.title: 6.4 Market Sizing and Trend Analysis
docs.text:
Analysts use two primary approaches to measure an industry's potential:

  • Top-Down Approach: Starts with macro-factors (e.g., total population) and narrows down to potential users and average expenditure.

  • Bottom-Up Approach: Aggregates the reported data of all individual companies in the sector to arrive at total industry revenue.

docs.title: 6.5 Secular Trends and Value Migration
docs.text:
Secular trends are long-term shifts (occurring once every 7–10 years) that permanently change how goods are produced or consumed.

Drivers of Secular Trends:

  • Technology: e.g., Digital cameras making film obsolete; Shale gas drilling lowering energy costs.

  • Demographics: e.g., An aging population in Japan reducing beer consumption.

  • Culture: e.g., Shift toward western clothing in Asia or organic foods.

Value Migration:

This happens when a phenomenon creates a long-term advantage for one entity at the cost of others.

  • Geographic: Value shifting to low-cost hubs like China.

  • Cross-Industry: e.g., Digital photography destroying the film roll industry (Kodak).

  • Across Value Chain: e.g., High competition in Indian telecom reducing carrier profits but benefiting digital content providers.

docs.title: I. Michael Porter’s Five Force Model
docs.text:
This model determines an industry's attractiveness and long-term profitability.

Force Impact on Profitability Industry Rivalry High rivalry (many players, standard products) leads to lower pricing power. Threat of Substitutes High if switching costs are low (e.g., SMS replacing Telegrams). Bargaining Power of Buyers High if there are many sellers and few buyers (e.g., Government as a buyer). Bargaining Power of Suppliers High if the input is critical or controlled by a few (e.g., OPEC for Crude Oil). Barriers to Entry (Moat) High barriers (licensing, high capital, strong brands) protect profits.

docs.title: II. PESTLE Analysis
docs.text:
Evaluates the external macro-environmental factors.

  • Political: Stability, corruption levels, and fiscal policy.

  • Economic: GDP contributors, inflation, interest rates, and trade balance.

  • Socio-Cultural: Demographics, lifestyle factors, and education.

  • Technological: R&D activity and digital infrastructure.

  • Legal: Transparency in legal architecture and enforcement of laws.

  • Environmental: Pollution control, waste disposal, and ESG compliance.

docs.title: III. BCG Matrix
docs.text:
Classifies business segments based on Market Growth and Market Share.

  • Stars: High growth, high share. Require investment but generate high cash.

  • Cash Cows: Low growth, high share. Stable, steady cash generators (e.g., Colgate, Navneet Publications).

  • Question Marks: High growth, low share. Risky; require strategy to become Stars.

  • Dogs: Low growth, low share. Low cash generation.

docs.title: 6.7 Key Industry Drivers and KPIs
docs.text: Industry Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) Airlines/Logistics Passenger/Cargo km, Occupancy rate, Price per km. Banking/NBFC NIM (Net Interest Margin), NPA Ratio, CASA Ratio, Capital Adequacy. IT Services FTE (Full Time Equivalent) billing, Attrition rate, Revenue per FTE. Retail Number of stores, Same-Store Sales Growth (SSSG). Telecom ARPU (Average Revenue Per User), Subscriber Churn rate.

docs.title: Direct Taxes
docs.text:
• Corporate Income Tax: Standard rate is 30% (or 25% for turnover below ₹400 cr).

  • MAT (Minimum Alternate Tax): Payable if income tax is less than 15% of book profits.

  • Surcharge: 12% if income is above ₹10 cr; 7% if between ₹1 cr and ₹10 cr.

  • Cess: 4% Health and Education cess.

docs.title: Indirect Taxes
docs.text:
• GST: Most goods are taxed at 18%.

  • Excise & VAT: Still applicable to liquor, petrol, and diesel.

  • STT (Securities Transaction Tax): Paid at the time of selling securities.

docs.title: Quick Facts for Revision
docs.text:
• The "Moat": A term popularized by Warren Buffett referring to high barriers to entry that protect a business from competitors.

  • Role Reversal: In SCP analysis, Structure determines Conduct, which in turn results in Performance (RoE, RoIC).

  • Road Tax: A lifetime tax paid upfront by automobile purchasers that can impact downstream auto-ancillary demand.

  • Going Concern: If a company is loss-making and a turnaround is unlikely, it is valued at liquidation value rather than EV/Sales.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Company Analysis – Business and Governance
docs.text: Company analysis is the final, granular level of the E-I-C (Economy-Industry-Company) framework. While macro and industry factors set the stage, company-specific factors determine which individual business will outperform its peers.

docs.title: 7.1 Role of Company Analysis in Fundamental Research
docs.text: Analysts focus on internal drivers such as business models, management quality, and competitive advantages to assess if a company can exploit industry opportunities and withstand external threats. This qualitative study provides the context needed before diving into the numerical financial analysis.

docs.title: 7.2 Understanding Business and Business Models
docs.text: Analysts must start with a fundamental question: "Do I understand the business?". - Core Logic: Research should prioritize firms whose products, customers, and delivery mechanisms are clear. - Sector Specificity: Each industry has unique KPIs. For example, Footfalls are critical for Retail, Net Interest Margin (NIM) for Banking, and Average Revenue Per User (ARPU) for Telecom. - Model vs. Product: Competition is often between business models (how value is created/delivered) rather than just the products themselves.

docs.title: 7.3 Pricing Power and Sustainability
docs.text: Pricing Power is the ability to independently determine prices without losing customers to competitors. - Drivers: It is influenced by industry factors (competition intensity) and company-specific factors like brand loyalty and a low-cost base. - Impact: Companies with high pricing power can pass on raw material cost escalations to customers, protecting their profit margins.

docs.title: 7.4 Competitive Advantages and Differentiation
docs.text:
To outperform, a company must distinguish itself in three primary areas:

Area of Differentiation Focus Key Driver Product Differentiation Unique features, quality, or functionality. Strong R&D and a culture of innovation. Competitive Pricing Offering better value for money than peers. Operational efficiency and a low-cost advantage. Execution Better branding, sales strategy, and positioning. Management track record and sales force focus.

docs.title: 7.5 SWOT Analysis Framework
docs.text:
SWOT analysis evaluates internal capabilities versus external dynamics.

  • Strengths (Internal): Financial strength, patents (IP), low customer concentration, and strong track record.
  • Weaknesses (Internal): High fixed costs, weak margins, high debt, or lack of experience in new segments.
  • Opportunities (External): Technological shifts, geographical expansion, or industry consolidation.
  • Threats (External): Economic recession, regulatory changes, or disruptive new technologies.

docs.title: 7.6 Quality of Management and Governance
docs.text: Because ownership is separate from management, Agency Risk exists—the risk that managers may not act in the best interest of owners.

docs.title: I. Evaluating Management Competency
docs.text: Analysts assess "C-level" executives based on: - Experience & Track Record: Past performance in similar roles. - Vision: Long-term strategic direction and goal-setting. - Execution: History of meeting or exceeding stated guidance. - Succession Planning: Plans for continuity if top management leaves.

docs.title: II. Corporate Governance Standards
docs.text: These are the rules and processes that ensure a company is run ethically. Key indicators include: - Board Composition: At least ⅓ to ½ of the board should be Independent Directors. - Role Separation: The Chairman of the Board should ideally not be the CEO/MD (mandated for the top 1,000 listed companies). - Auditor Integrity: Auditors should be rotated every 5 years and not be overly dependent on the fees from a single group. - Related Party Transactions: Transactions with promoter-owned entities must be at "arms-length" and reviewed by the audit committee.

docs.title: 7.7 Business Risks
docs.text: Analysts must constantly ask: "What could go wrong?". A good management team is transparent about risks—such as currency fluctuations or execution delays—and has mitigation strategies in place.

docs.title: 7.8 Credit Rating History
docs.text: A company's Credit Rating indicates its ability to service debt. Tracking changes in these ratings over time reveals financial risk levels and how responsive management is to the concerns raised by rating agencies.

docs.title: 7.9 ESG Framework (Environment, Social, and Governance)
docs.text: Modern investors use ESG filters to identify sustainable businesses. - Environmental: Carbon footprint, pollution control, and resource efficiency. - Social: Human rights, gender equality, and community relations. - Governance: Ethics and shareholder rights. - Regulatory Note: SEBI now mandates top 1,000 companies to provide ESG disclosures via the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR).

docs.title: Quick Facts for Revision
docs.text:
• Moat: A term for high entry barriers that protect a company's "economic castle".
  • Promoter Pledging: Promoters may take loans against their shares; high pledging can lead to sharp price drops if lenders are forced to sell the collateral.
  • BRSR: The official framework for ESG reporting in India starting FY2023.
  • Arms-Length: A principle requiring transactions between related parties to be conducted as if they were between independent entities.
  • Keyman Risk: The risk to an organization if its leadership is too concentrated in a few individuals without a succession plan.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Company Analysis – Financial Analysis
docs.text: Financial analysis translates qualitative business assessments into numerical expectations. It involves studying a company’s historical performance to forecast its future ability to generate profits and cash flows.

docs.title: 8.1 Introduction to Financial Statements
docs.text: Financial statements are prepared under accrual accounting, where income is recognized when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands. Under IndAS 1, a complete set includes: - Balance Sheet: Financial position at a specific point in time. - Profit and Loss (P/L) Statement: Financial performance over a period. - Statement of Changes in Equity: Movements in shareholder funds. - Cash Flow Statement: Sources and uses of cash. - Notes to Accounts: Detailed explanations of accounting policies and breakdowns of line items.

docs.title: 8.2 Consolidated vs. Stand-alone Results
docs.text:
• Stand-alone Financials: Represent the financial position of the parent entity alone.
  • Consolidated Financials: Treat a parent company and all its controlled subsidiaries as a single economic unit.
  • Key Insight: Analysts generally prefer consolidated statements as they provide a holistic view of the entire business group's performance.

docs.title: 8.3 The Balance Sheet
docs.text: The balance sheet follows the equation: \(\text{Assets} = \text{Equity} + \text{Liabilities}\).

docs.title: I. Common Asset Classifications
docs.text: Category Definition Key Line Items Non-Current Assets Benefits expected beyond one year. Property, Plant & Equipment (PPE), Goodwill, Intangible Assets, Long-term Investments. Current Assets Benefits expected within one operating cycle (typically one year). Inventory, Trade Receivables, Cash & Cash Equivalents, Short-term Investments.

docs.title: II. Equity and Liabilities
docs.text:
• Equity: Represents residual interest belonging to owners (Share Capital + Reserves).
  • Non-Current Liabilities: Long-term obligations like term loans and bonds due beyond one year.
  • Current Liabilities: Obligations due within one year, such as Trade Payables, short-term debt, and the current portion of long-term debt.

docs.title: III. Balance Sheet Metrics
docs.text:
• Total Debt: Sum of long-term debt, short-term debt, lease obligations, and current maturities.
  • Working Capital: \(\text{Current Assets} - \text{Current Liabilities}\).
  • Core Working Capital: \(\text{Inventory} + \text{Trade Receivables} - \text{Trade Payables}\). This measures the capital required to sustain core operations.

docs.title: 8.4 The Profit and Loss (P/L) Account
docs.text: The P/L account reveals a company's ability to generate value from its operations.

docs.title: I. Key Profit Metrics
docs.text:
• EBITDA: Earning Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation, and Amortization. It measures operating efficiency without the impact of capital structure or non-cash charges.
  • EBIT (Operating Profit): EBITDA minus Depreciation and Amortization. Used to measure the ability to service interest.
  • PAT (Net Profit): Final profit available to shareholders after all expenses and taxes.

docs.title: II. Adjusted Profit after Tax
docs.text: Analysts calculate Adjusted PAT by removing the impact of Exceptional Items (one-time, non-recurring events) to understand the company's true sustainable earning power.

docs.title: 8.5 Basics of Cash Flows
docs.text: Cash flows are segregated into three distinct streams: 1. Operating Cash Flows: Cash generated from core business activities (e.g., selling goods). Warning: Continuous negative operating cash flow is an alarming signal of risk. 2. Investing Cash Flows: Cash used for or generated from assets (e.g., buying machinery or selling land). 3. Financing Cash Flows: Cash related to capital structure (e.g., borrowing loans or paying dividends).

docs.title: 8.6 Quality of Accounting: Audit Reports
docs.text: An auditor reviews the financial statements and provides one of three opinions: - Clean Report: No issues found; reflects a "true and fair" view. - Qualified Report: The auditor has specific reservations about certain accounting treatments. - Disclaimer: The auditor is unable to verify parts of the financials due to a lack of information.

docs.title: I. Profitability and Return Ratios
docs.text: Ratio Formula Significance EBITDA Margin \(\text{EBITDA} / \text{Net Sales}\) Measures operating efficiency. Return on Equity (ROE) \(\text{Net Profit} / \text{Average Net-worth}\) Single most important metric for equity investors. Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) \(\text{EBIT} / \text{Average Total Capital}\) Measures overall capital productivity (Equity + Debt).

docs.title: II. Leverage and Liquidity Ratios
docs.text: Ratio Formula Significance Debt/Equity \(\text{Total Debt} / \text{Net-worth}\) Measures financial risk; ideally \(\le 1\). Interest Coverage \(\text{EBIT} / \text{Interest Expense}\) Ability to pay interest from earnings. Current Ratio \(\text{Current Assets} / \text{Current Liabilities}\) Ability to meet short-term obligations. Quick Ratio \((\text{Current Assets} - \text{Inventory}) / \text{Current Liabilities}\) Measures immediate liquidity.

docs.title: 8.8 Dupont Analysis
docs.text: Dupont Analysis decomposes ROE into three drivers to identify how a company is generating returns: $\(\text{ROE} = \text{Net Profit Margin} \times \text{Asset Turnover} \times \text{Financial Leverage}\)$ - Insight: If ROE increases due to higher leverage rather than margin or efficiency, it signals higher risk.

docs.title: Quick Facts for Revision
docs.text:
• Accrual Basis: Profits in the P/L do not equal cash in the bank.
  • Goodwill: Arises when an acquisition price exceeds the fair value of net assets.
  • Contingent Liabilities: Potential obligations recorded in notes (e.g., lawsuits) but not on the balance sheet.
  • Inventory Turnover: Higher is better; it indicates how fast stock is converted into sales.
  • Insider Activity: If insiders are buying, it is often a strong signal of future profit potential.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Terminology in Equity and Debt Markets
docs.text: No. Term / Description 1 Equity Share Capital – The nominal or par value of the company's ownership capital, calculated as shares issued multiplied by face value. \(\text{Equity Share Capital} = \text{Number of Shares Issued} \times \text{Face Value}\) 2 Book Value Per Share – The theoretical amount each share would receive if the company were liquidated, derived from net worth divided by outstanding shares. \(\text{Book Value Per Share} = \frac{\text{Net Worth}}{\text{Number of Outstanding Shares}}\) 3 Market Capitalization – The total market value of a company's outstanding equity, calculated as market price per share times total shares. \(\text{Market Cap} = \text{Market Price Per Share} \times \text{Total Outstanding Shares}\) 4 Enterprise Value (Standalone) – The total cost to acquire the entire business, reflecting its capital structure; calculated as equity plus debt minus cash. \(\text{EV} = (\text{Market Value of Equity} + \text{Market Value of Debt}) - \text{Cash and Equivalents}\) 5 Earnings Per Share (EPS) – The profit earned for each outstanding share of common stock. \(\text{EPS} = \frac{\text{Net Profit}}{\text{Number of Shares Outstanding}}\) 6 Dividend Payout Ratio – The percentage of net income distributed to shareholders as dividends. \(\text{Dividend Payout Ratio} = \frac{\text{Dividend Per Share}}{\text{EPS}}\) 7 Price to Earnings (PE) Ratio – A valuation multiple showing how much investors pay per rupee of earnings. \(\text{PE Ratio} = \frac{\text{Market Price Per Share}}{\text{EPS}}\) 8 Price to Sales (P/S) Ratio – A valuation metric useful for companies with negative earnings or temporary losses. \(\text{P/S Ratio} = \frac{\text{Market Capitalization}}{\text{Annual Net Sales}}\) 9 Price to Book Value (P/BV) Ratio – Compares market price to the accounting (book) value of the company's assets. \(\text{P/BV Ratio} = \frac{\text{Current Market Price}}{\text{Book Value Per Share}}\) 10 Current Yield (Bonds) – A simple measure of a bond's annual income return based on its current market price. \(\text{Current Yield} = \frac{\text{Annual Coupon}}{\text{Current Market Price}}\) 11 Holding Period Return (HPR) – The total return earned from an investment over the period it was held, including coupon, reinvestment income, and price change. \(\text{HPR} = \frac{\text{Coupon} + \text{Reinvestment Income} + (\text{Sale Price} - \text{Purchase Price})}{\text{Purchase Price}}\) 12 Modified Duration – Measures a bond's price sensitivity to a 1% change in interest rates, where \(y\) is the yield. \(\text{Modified Duration} = \frac{\text{Macaulay's Duration}}{(1 + y)}\)

docs.title: Chapter 5: Economic Analysis
docs.text: No. Term / Description 1 Per Capita Income – A measure of the average standard of living and economic output per person in a country. \(\text{Per Capita Income} = \frac{\text{National Income}}{\text{Total Population}}\)

docs.title: Chapter 8: Company Analysis – Financial Analysis
docs.text: No. Term / Description 1 EBITDA Margin – Evaluates operational efficiency by excluding non-cash and financing costs from the profitability measure. \(\text{EBITDA Margin} = \frac{\text{EBITDA}}{\text{Net Sales}}\) 2 PAT Margin – Measures the final residual profit margin left for shareholders after all costs, including taxes. \(\text{PAT Margin} = \frac{\text{Profit After Tax}}{\text{Net Sales}}\) 3 Return on Equity (ROE) – Shows how efficiently management uses shareholder capital to generate profit. \(\text{ROE} = \frac{\text{Net Profit}}{\text{Average Net Worth}}\) 4 Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) – Measures the return generated on both debt and equity capital employed in the business. \(\text{ROCE} = \frac{\text{EBIT}}{\text{Average Capital Employed}}\) 5 Debt/Equity (D/E) Ratio – Assesses the financial leverage and risk level of a company by comparing total debt to net worth. \(\text{D/E Ratio} = \frac{\text{Total Adjusted Debt}}{\text{Net Worth}}\) 6 Interest Coverage Ratio – Determines how easily a company can pay interest on its outstanding debt from operating profits. \(\text{Interest Coverage} = \frac{\text{EBIT}}{\text{Interest Expense}}\) 7 Current Ratio – Evaluates a firm's ability to meet short-term obligations using its current assets. \(\text{Current Ratio} = \frac{\text{Current Assets}}{\text{Current Liabilities}}\) 8 Quick Ratio – A stricter liquidity test focusing on assets that convert to cash immediately, excluding inventories. \(\text{Quick Ratio} = \frac{\text{Current Assets} - \text{Inventories}}{\text{Current Liabilities}}\) 9 Dupont Analysis (ROE) – Decomposes ROE into three components (profitability, efficiency, and leverage) to identify the drivers of returns. \(\text{ROE} = \text{Net Profit Margin} \times \text{Asset Turnover} \times \text{Equity Multiplier}\)

docs.title: Chapter 10: Valuation Principles
docs.text: No. Term / Description 1 Gordon Growth Model (GGM) – Values a stock based on a perpetual stream of dividends growing at a constant rate, where \(P_0\) is price, \(D_1\) is next dividend, \(k\) is discount rate, and \(g\) is growth rate. \(P_0 = \frac{D_1}{(k - g)}\) 2 Cost of Equity (CAPM) – Calculates required return on equity using the risk-free rate (\(R_f\)), beta (\(\beta\)), and market risk premium (\(R_m - R_f\)). \(K_e = R_f + \beta \times (R_m - R_f)\) 3 Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) – The average cost of all capital sources (equity and debt) used by a firm, where \(W_e\) and \(W_d\) are weights of equity and debt. \(\text{WACC} = [K_e \times W_e] + [K_d \times (1 - \text{Tax}) \times W_d]\) 4 PEG Ratio – Adjusts the PE ratio to account for the company's expected earnings growth rate, providing a growth-adjusted valuation metric. \(\text{PEG Ratio} = \frac{\text{PE Ratio}}{\text{Growth Rate}}\)

docs.title: Chapter 11: Fundamental Analysis of Commodities
docs.text: No. Term / Description 1 Hedge Ratio – Determines the optimal number of futures contracts to hedge a spot position, where \(\rho\) is correlation and SD is standard deviation of spot and futures price changes. \(\text{Hedge Ratio} = \rho \times \left( \frac{\text{SD}_{\text{Spot}}}{\text{SD}_{\text{Futures}}} \right)\)

docs.title: Chapter 12: Fundamentals of Risk and Return
docs.text: No. Term / Description 1 Return on Investment (ROI) – A basic measure of profitability for a single period, expressed as a percentage of the investment. \(\text{ROI} = \left( \frac{\text{Net Profit}}{\text{Investment}} \right) \times 100\) 2 Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) – The smoothened annual growth rate of an investment over a multi-year period, where \(n\) is the number of years. \(\text{CAGR} = \left( \frac{\text{End Value}}{\text{Beginning Value}} \right)^{\frac{1}{n}} - 1\) 3 Sharpe Ratio – Measures excess return earned per unit of total risk (standard deviation, \(\sigma_p\)), where \(R_p\) is portfolio return and \(R_f\) is risk-free rate. \(\text{Sharpe Ratio} = \frac{(R_p - R_f)}{\sigma_p}\) 4 Treynor Ratio – Measures excess return earned per unit of systematic risk (Beta, \(\beta_p\)), useful for evaluating diversified portfolios. \(\text{Treynor Ratio} = \frac{(R_p - R_f)}{\beta_p}\) 5 Jensen's Alpha – Quantifies the active return added by a portfolio manager above the expected market return based on CAPM. \(\alpha = R_p - [R_f + \beta_p \times (R_m - R_f)]\)

docs.title: Should we learn all these formulae?
docs.text: Based on the official NISM syllabus, you will need to understand and apply these formulas, not just memorize them in isolation. The exam tests your ability to use them in practical scenarios.

docs.title: Exam Structure and Application
docs.text:
The NISM Research Analyst exam has a specific structure designed to test applied knowledge .

  • Exam Format: 80 multiple-choice questions (1 mark each) and 5 case-based questions (each with 4 sub-questions of 1 mark). The case-based questions are particularly important as they will test your ability to apply formulas to real-world problems .
  • Important Weightage: The topics where many of these formulas are concentrated carry significant weight.
    • Chapter 8 (Company Analysis – Financial Analysis): 16% weightage .
    • Chapter 10 (Valuation Principles): 16% weightage .

Given this high weightage, you can expect direct and application-based questions from these chapters.

docs.title: "Memorization" vs. "Understanding and Application"
docs.text:
It's crucial to know when and how to use each formula. The official syllabus for Chapter 8 states that candidates must "Know the computation of Dupont Analysis" and "Know the commonly used ratios used in financial analysis," which clearly requires more than just rote learning .

Here is how you should approach each formula in your tables:

  • Chapter 3 (Terminology): These are foundational. You'll need to know the formulas for Market Cap, EPS, PE Ratio, and Current Yield to interpret market data and answer basic questions.
  • Chapter 8 (Financial Analysis): This is where application is key. You should be prepared to calculate ratios (like ROE, ROCE, D/E, Current Ratio) from a set of financial data and interpret what they mean about a company's health.
  • Chapter 10 (Valuation): You must understand how to use the Gordon Growth Model, CAPM, and WACC. These are core to valuing companies and are frequently tested in application-based scenarios.
  • Chapter 12 (Risk and Return): Expect questions that ask you to calculate the Sharpe Ratio or CAGR for a portfolio, not just define it.

In short, your current work in organizing these formulas is an excellent first step. The next step is to practice applying them to examples and case studies, as that is exactly how you will be tested.

docs.title: Participants of the Financial Market
docs.text:
The financial market functions as an ecosystem where funds move from those who have surplus money to those who need money. This ecosystem operates efficiently because of the interaction among four key participants:

Participant Role Investors / Providers of Funds Supply capital by purchasing securities Borrowers / Seekers of Funds Raise capital by issuing securities Intermediaries Facilitate issuance, trading, settlement, and safekeeping of securities Regulatory Bodies Ensure fairness, transparency, stability, and investor protection

docs.title: 1. Investors / Providers of Funds
docs.text: Investors are the source of capital in the financial system. They invest their savings with the expectation of earning returns through dividends, interest, capital appreciation, or a combination of these.

docs.title: 1.1 Retail Investors
docs.text:
These are individual investors investing their personal savings.

Examples:

  • Salaried employees
  • Business owners
  • Professionals
  • Retired individuals

Typical investments:

  • Shares
  • Mutual Funds
  • Bonds
  • ETFs
  • Government Securities

docs.title: 1.2 Institutional Investors
docs.text:
These organizations manage large pools of money.

Examples:

docs.title: Domestic Institutional Investors (DIIs)
docs.text:
• Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC)
  • Mutual Funds
  • Pension Funds
  • Insurance Companies

Examples of Mutual Fund Houses:

  • SBI Mutual Fund
  • HDFC Mutual Fund
  • ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund

docs.title: 1.3 Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs)
docs.text:
Foreign investors investing in Indian securities.

Examples:

  • Global pension funds
  • Sovereign wealth funds
  • Foreign mutual funds
  • Hedge funds

Examples:

  • BlackRock
  • Vanguard Group
  • Government Pension Fund Global

docs.title: Why Investors Matter
docs.text:
Without investors:

  • Companies cannot raise capital.
  • Governments cannot borrow efficiently.
  • Economic growth slows down.

Investors are therefore the suppliers of capital to the economy.

docs.title: 2. Borrowers / Seekers of Funds
docs.text: Borrowers are entities that require money for expansion, operations, infrastructure development, or government spending.

docs.title: 2.1 Corporates
docs.text: Companies raise funds through:

docs.title: Equity
docs.text:
By issuing:

  • IPOs
  • FPOs
  • Rights Issues

Examples:

  • Reliance Industries
  • Tata Consultancy Services
  • Infosys

docs.title: 2.2 Government
docs.text:
Governments borrow for:

  • Infrastructure projects
  • Welfare schemes
  • Budget deficits

Through:

  • Treasury Bills (T-Bills)
  • Government Securities (G-Secs)
  • State Development Loans (SDLs)

Examples:

  • Government of India
  • State Governments

docs.title: 2.3 Financial Institutions
docs.text:
Banks and financial institutions also raise funds through debt instruments.

Examples:

  • State Bank of India
  • HDFC Bank
  • Power Finance Corporation

docs.title: Why Borrowers Matter
docs.text:
Borrowers use the capital raised to:

  • Build factories
  • Expand businesses
  • Create jobs
  • Develop infrastructure

Thus, they convert savings into productive economic activity.

docs.title: 3. Intermediaries
docs.text:
Intermediaries provide the infrastructure that makes the securities market function smoothly.

Without intermediaries, investors and issuers would struggle to find each other, trade securely, or settle transactions.

docs.title: 3.1 Stock Exchanges
docs.text:
Stock exchanges provide a regulated platform where securities are bought and sold.

Major Indian Stock Exchanges:

docs.title: National Stock Exchange of India (NSE)
docs.text:
• Largest stock exchange in India
  • Benchmark Index: Nifty 50

docs.title: BSE Limited (BSE)
docs.text:
• Asia's oldest stock exchange
  • Benchmark Index: Sensex

Functions:

  • Trading platform
  • Price discovery
  • Market surveillance
  • Transparency

docs.title: 3.2 Stock Brokers
docs.text:
Brokers act as intermediaries between investors and stock exchanges.

Examples:

  • Zerodha
  • Groww
  • Angel One
  • ICICI Direct

Functions:

  • Trade execution
  • Research
  • Advisory
  • Trading platforms

docs.title: 3.3 Depositories
docs.text:
Depositories hold securities in electronic (demat) form.

India has two depositories:

docs.title: National Securities Depository Limited (NSDL)
docs.text: Established in 1996.

docs.title: Central Depository Services Limited (CDSL)
docs.text:
Established in 1999.

Functions:

  • Hold securities electronically
  • Facilitate transfer of ownership
  • Enable dematerialization

Think of a depository as a bank for securities.

docs.title: 3.4 Depository Participants (DPs)
docs.text:
Investors cannot directly open accounts with NSDL/CDSL.

Instead they open demat accounts through DPs.

Examples:

  • Banks
  • Brokers
  • Financial institutions

Examples:

  • SBI Securities
  • HDFC Securities
  • Zerodha

docs.title: 3.5 Clearing Corporations
docs.text:
Clearing corporations ensure that every trade is settled successfully.

Major clearing corporations:

docs.title: National Securities Clearing Corporation Limited (NSCCL)
docs.text: Associated with NSE.

docs.title: Indian Clearing Corporation Limited (ICCL)
docs.text:
Associated with BSE.

Functions:

  • Guarantee settlement
  • Manage counterparty risk
  • Collect margins
  • Ensure delivery of securities and funds

docs.title: 3.6 Merchant Bankers
docs.text:
Merchant bankers help companies raise capital.

Functions:

  • IPO management
  • Due diligence
  • Prospectus preparation
  • Regulatory compliance

Examples:

  • ICICI Securities
  • Axis Capital
  • Kotak Mahindra Capital Company

docs.title: 3.7 Credit Rating Agencies
docs.text:
These agencies assess the creditworthiness of debt issuers.

Examples:

  • CRISIL
  • ICRA
  • CARE Ratings

docs.title: 4. Regulatory Bodies
docs.text: Regulators maintain market integrity and protect investors.

docs.title: 4.1 SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India)
Securities and Exchange Board of India
docs.text:
SEBI is the primary regulator of the Indian securities market.

Functions:

  • Protect investors
  • Regulate intermediaries
  • Prevent market manipulation
  • Approve public issues
  • Develop securities markets

For a Research Analyst, SEBI is the most important regulator.

docs.title: Reserve Bank of India
docs.text:
Functions:

  • Monetary policy
  • Banking regulation
  • Government debt management
  • Currency management

docs.title: Ministry of Finance
docs.text:
Functions:

  • Financial legislation
  • Fiscal policy
  • Capital market policy oversight

docs.title: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India
docs.text:
Regulates:

  • Insurance companies
  • Insurance products

docs.title: Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority
docs.text:
Regulates:

  • Pension funds
  • National Pension System (NPS)

docs.title: How All Participants Work Together (Exam Perspective)
docs.text:
A useful flow to remember is:

Investors → Brokers → Stock Exchange → Clearing Corporation → Depository → Borrowers/Issuers

For example:

  1. A company such as Reliance needs ₹10,000 crore.
  2. It issues securities through the market.
  3. Merchant bankers manage the issue.
  4. Investors subscribe through brokers.
  5. Shares are credited to demat accounts via NSDL/CDSL.
  6. NSE/BSE enable trading.
  7. Clearing corporations guarantee settlement.
  8. SEBI supervises the entire ecosystem.

This flow represents the complete life cycle of capital movement in the Indian securities market and is a favorite area for conceptual NISM questions.

docs.title: Study Plan
docs.text:
Preparation Strategy

To help you study in parallel, I’ve refined the tracks into thematic pillars. This allows you to work through different "mindsets"—Regulatory, Internal Analysis, and External Trends—simultaneously without feeling repetitive.

docs.title: Track 1: Market Mechanics & Regulation (35 Marks)
docs.text:
Focus: How the market is built, governed, and analyzed via price action.

  • Ch 1: Intro to RA Profession (1)
  • Ch 2: Intro to Securities Market (2)
  • Ch 3: Terminology in Equity and Debt (2)
  • Ch 4: Fundamentals of Research (5)
  • Ch 14: Legal and Regulatory Environment (10)
  • Ch 15: Technical Analysis (15)

docs.title: Track 2: The Company Pillar (35 Marks)
docs.text:
Focus: Deep-diving into the business itself and determining what it is worth.

  • Ch 7: Company Analysis – Business and Governance (6)
  • Ch 8: Company Analysis – Financial Analysis (12)
  • Ch 10: Valuation Principles (12)
  • Ch 13: Qualities of a Good Research Report (5)

docs.title: Track 3: Macro & Risk Pillar (30 Marks)
docs.text:
Focus: Broad economic drivers and the math of managing risk.

  • Ch 5: Economic Analysis (5)
  • Ch 6: Industry Analysis (8)
  • Ch 9: Corporate Actions (5)
  • Ch 11: Fundamental Analysis of Commodities (5)
  • Ch 12: Fundamentals of Risk and Return (7)

docs.title: Logic of Parallel Learning
docs.text: These tracks are designed so that you can switch between them to avoid fatigue. Track 1 is largely rules-based, Track 2 is math/accounting-heavy, and Track 3 is conceptual/macro-focused.

docs.title: Interdependencies
docs.text:
While they are parallel, there are three critical "bridge" chapters you should handle first:

  1. Chapter 3 (Terminology): You must understand the basic terms here before you can effectively analyze financials in Track 2 or economics in Track 3.

  2. Chapter 4 (Research Fundamentals): This introduces the "Top-Down" vs. "Bottom-Up" approaches, which are the primary connection points between Track 2 (Company) and Track 3 (Macro/Industry).

  3. Chapter 8 (Financials) \(\rightarrow\) Chapter 10 (Valuation): In Track 2, you cannot do Valuation effectively without first mastering the Financial Analysis in Chapter 8.

docs.title: Weeky Plan
docs.text:
This 3-week parallel study plan is logically arranged to build foundational vocabulary first, followed by the "Top-Down" analytical framework, and ending with complex valuation and regulatory requirements.

The logic uses Track 1 for rules and mechanics, Track 2 for internal business health, and Track 3 for external macro influences.

docs.title: Logical Arrangement & Interdependencies
docs.text:
• Week 1 (The Foundation): Focuses on basic terminology (Ch 3) and the Top-Down research logic (Ch 4) before diving into deep math.
  • Week 2 (Data & Trends): Pairs the intensive study of financial statements (Ch 8) with price-action analysis (Ch 15). Understanding industry drivers (Ch 6) helps contextualize the company's financial performance.
